newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan's Islamists say they boycotting elections.
newsitem.headline: Jordan's Islamists say they boycotting elections.

text.p: Jordan's biggest political party the Islamist Action Front said on Thursday it would boycott parliamentary elections due to be held later this year.

Meeting a day after King Hussein told his government to prepare for the elections, the party's consultative council voted overwhelming to support a boycott call by the influential Moslem Brotherhood movement.
"After the parties and political forces decided to boycott we had to review our decision to participate," said Adnan Majali, head of the consultative council which sets policy for the Front.

Four small secular parties have already said they will boycott the elections, saying a succession of governments appointed by King Hussein have marginalised the role of parliament and particularly the opposition.
The elections would be the first since Jordan's 1994 peace treaty with Israel, which the Islamic and secular opposition regard as a capitulation and want to see revoked.

The Islamic Action Front, a political arm of the Brotherhood established five years ago, won 16 of the 80 parliamentary seats in the last elections in 1993, making it the biggest single party in that parliament. It enjoys wide grassroots support.

Along with a handful of pan-Arab and leftist parliamentary deputies it tried unsuccessfully to block ratification of the peace accord with Israel and also wants the government to revoke interim laws on the press, the economy and the elections which were issued during a parliamentary recess.

Prime Minister Abdul-Salam al-Majali is expected to set a date next week for the elections, which must be held within four years of the last elections in November 1993. He has promised they will be free and fair.
The government has said it would like the Islamists to take part but described their demands as illogical and said the elections would go ahead with or without them.
Adnan Majali said the Islamic Action Front's decision could be reviewed "if the party found that the reasons which called for the boycott no longer exist".
"We don't want a crisis," he told Reuters.
But most supporters of the boycott say the government has no plans to address their complaints.
"It is not in the government's plans to respond to our demands," said IAF deputy Abdul-Moneim Abu Zunt, a keen advocate of the boycott.
He said a boycott by the Islamists would remove any democratic credentials from Jordan's parliament.
"The opposition is the spirit of democracy. Parliament without opposition is a body without soul," Abu Zunt said.
